title: What time is it? — time, days, dates
title_target: Bây giờ là mấy giờ rồi?
goal: Tell the time, the day and the date — and keep apart two words that English squeezes into one: "hour" as a point on the clock and "hour" as a length of time.
bekal: tell the full time with *rưỡi*, *kém* and the part of the day
name the days of the week — which are numbered starting from two
say the date, month and year in Vietnamese order: day, then month, then year

notes: **Good news first: *hai giờ rưỡi* means 2:30, just like English "half past two"** — literally "two hour half". Vietnamese names the hour that has **already passed** and adds the half, the same way English does. (Learners who know German or Dutch, where *halb drei* means 2:30, have to unlearn something; you don't.)

**Giờ and tiếng both mean "hour", but they can't be swapped.** *Giờ* is a **point in time**: *ba giờ* (three o'clock). *Tiếng* is a **length of time**: *ba tiếng* (three hours). English uses one word for both, so the mistake is natural — but *tôi học ba giờ* means "I study at three o'clock", while *tôi học ba tiếng* means "I study for three hours".

**The part of the day goes AFTER the hour**: *ba giờ chiều* (three in the afternoon), *bảy giờ tối* (seven in the evening), *sáu giờ sáng* (six in the morning). Like English "3 p.m.", and for the same reason Vietnamese almost always tells time on a twelve-hour clock, not a twenty-four-hour one.

**Lúc means "at" for time**, and it's needed before the hour in both questions and answers: *lúc mấy giờ?* (at what time?), *lúc ba giờ* (at three o'clock). Without *lúc* the sentence is still understood, but sounds like a timetable entry, not a sentence.

**The days of the week are numbered, and the numbers start at TWO.** *Thứ hai* (literally "second in order") is Monday, because Sunday counts as the first day — but Sunday has its own name, *chủ nhật*, not *thứ nhất*. So there's no *thứ nhất* on a Vietnamese calendar at all.

**Chúc mừng means "congratulations, happy …"** and is used for anything worth celebrating: *chúc mừng sinh nhật* (happy birthday), *chúc mừng năm mới* (happy new year). Its cousin *chúc* alone means "wish": *chúc anh ngủ ngon* (sleep well).

grammars.title: Telling the time
body: The pattern: **number + giờ + (minutes) + part of the day**. For minutes past the half hour, Vietnamese can use *kém* ("less"), just like English "quarter to".
after: ⚠️ Look again at the **3:30** row: *rưỡi* comes **after** *giờ*, never before it. *Ba giờ rưỡi* — not *rưỡi ba giờ*. And *rưỡi* is only for the half hour; for 2:30 you can also hear *hai giờ ba mươi* (two hour thirty).

Parts of the day: *sáng* (dawn–11), *trưa* (11–1, lunch & nap time), *chiều* (1–6), *tối* (6–10), *đêm* (late night). ⚠️ *Trưa* has no exact English match — it's not "afternoon" in general but **the middle of the day**, when shops close and people take a short nap.

grammars.title: Days, dates, months
body: Days are numbered, months are numbered, and dates are written from small to large — day, month, year.
after: ⚠️ Wednesday uses ***tư***, not *bốn* — the only day whose number changes form. It comes from the number-4 exception you saw in Unit 4.

Months have no names of their own: just *tháng* + the number. *Tháng một* = January, *tháng chín* = September, *tháng mười hai* = December. The only exception: in the traditional lunar calendar, the twelfth month is sometimes called *tháng chạp* and the first *tháng giêng*.

sections.title: From what time to what time

head: Tiếng Việt
Say it
English
rows: Từ chín giờ đến năm giờ
Từ chín zờ dến năm zờ

blocks.text: *Từ … đến …* ("from … to …") works for both time and place: *từ Hà Nội đến Huế* = "from Hà Nội to Huế". One frame, two uses, in the same order as English.
⚠️ *Muộn* (north) and *trễ* (south) both mean "late". If you're late, the full sentence is *Xin lỗi, tôi đến muộn.* — and in Vietnam it really is used; punctuality for work matters.

blocks.title: Tết — the week Vietnam stops
items: *Tết Nguyên Đán* is the lunar new year, falling between late January and mid-February. For about a week **almost every shop, office and food stall closes**, and the whole country goes home to family. If you're planning a trip to Vietnam, check the dates first — this is no ordinary holiday.

The greetings: *Chúc mừng năm mới!* (Happy New Year) and *Chúc mừng năm mới, an khang thịnh vượng!* (wishing you health and prosperity). Children are given *lì xì* — lucky money in red envelopes — just as at Chinese New Year.

exercises.prompt: Translate into English. Watch out for *giờ* and *tiếng*.
items: Bây giờ là năm giờ rưỡi.
Lớp bắt đầu lúc ba giờ chiều.
Chủ nhật này là sinh nhật chị.
Tôi học tiếng Việt hai ____ mỗi ngày.
Đi từ Hà Nội đến Huế mất mười hai ____.

answers: bảy giờ sáng — chín giờ rưỡi — ba giờ chiều — tám giờ mười lăm tối — năm giờ kém mười lăm — mười hai giờ rưỡi
It's half past five. — The class starts at three in the afternoon. — I study for three hours. — Today is Wednesday. — This Sunday is my birthday.
Bây giờ là mấy giờ? — Hôm nay là thứ mấy? — Hôm nay là ngày mười lăm tháng chín. — Từ chín giờ đến năm giờ. — Chúc mừng sinh nhật! — Xin lỗi, tôi đến muộn.
